Delos. A small island in the Aegean Sea at the center of the Cyclades, it was a sacred sanctuary dedicated as the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis. Though tiny and barren, Delos held immense religious significance across the Greek world and later served as the treasury of the Delian League, Athens's maritime alliance.

Delos was the sacred birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, the divine twins born to Leto on the island. Greek pilgrims traveled from across the Mediterranean to worship at the sanctuary. According to mythology, the island was once drifting until Poseidon fixed it in place so that Leto could find refuge to give birth. This act made Delos the holiest of sanctuaries.

The island housed the Temple of Apollo, which featured a famous archaic marble statue of the god. Visitors traveled far seeking divine favor and purification at this holy site. Delos served as the treasury and religious center of the Delian League from 478 to 404 BCE, an Athenian-led naval alliance against the Persians. Tribute from the allied cities was stored in the temple of Apollo.

The island contained an ancient harbor and became a major trading post and emporium despite its small size, due to its sacred status and central location in the Aegean. Delos housed the tombs and monuments of pilgrims, making it not only a religious destination but also a burial ground for the pious who wished to be interred in this holy place.

The island was virtually abandoned by the second century CE and fell into obscurity until archaeological excavations in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries revealed its former splendor. Apollo was born on the island and honored at its primary sanctuary. Artemis, Apollo's twin sister, was also born on Delos and honored there. Leto, their mother, gave birth to the divine twins on this sacred island.
